beats.text: So far, you've started every command yourself. Now let your PC do it, {something}the moment something happens.
Let's see {how}how events work, {real}some real ones, and how {cond}conditions make them smarter.
So far, you trigger the commands. {events}Events let your PC trigger them for you. {when}When this happens, run these commands.

There are {sixteen}twenty-two kinds of triggers. When K-Desktop {start}starts or exits. {time}At a time, or every few {interval}minutes. When a {program}program opens, or comes to the {front}front. After a while {idle}without using the PC. When you {lock}lock it, or it goes to sleep. When a laptop switches to {battery}battery.

When a {controller}controller, a {usb}USB drive, {headphones}headphones or any other device is connected. When you join a {network}network. When a new {file}file appears in a folder. When the {cpu}CPU, the graphics card or the memory crosses a threshold. Or when {remote}another computer, a script or Home Assistant calls it by name.

And a few more: when the {level}battery runs low, at {sun}sunrise or sunset, when a {screen}screen is plugged in, before a {calendar}calendar event, when {mail}mail arrives, or a {telegram}Telegram message.
For example: {when}when Steam opens, {switch}switch the audio output to the headphones.
Many triggers also have a {ends}When it ends side. {closes}When Steam closes, {back}back to the speakers. {nosecond}No second event needed.
Events can have {conditions}conditions, a {cooldown}minimum time between runs, and built-in {loops}protection against loops, so an event can never keep setting itself off.

Here are some real ones. {elden}When Elden Ring opens. {weekday}Every weekday at eight thirty. {away}When I step away. {headphones}When the headphones connect. A {file}new file in Downloads. And the {cpu}CPU above ninety percent.

Open one, and you see its {when}When: a program opens, {exe}Elden Ring. What it {runs}runs: Gaming mode, for high performance. And {ends}When it ends, to put things back. {test}Test runs it right away.

One last tip: in {only}Only if, add conditions. Then an event fires only when, say, it's a {weekday}weekday and you're on your {home}home network. Ask for {all}all of them, or any, and {check}test whether they're met right now.
Next up: {next}windows, the clipboard and the screen.
